en.sup: Supplied in English. The Greek says 'kept back from the price'.
Supplied in English. The Greek gives 'laid' no object.

01.r: Continues the account of Ananias from the verse before.

02.r: He secretly kept some of the money for himself.
02.n: Abbott-Smith derives it from νόσφι, 'apart, aside', and gives the middle, the form here, as 'to set apart for oneself, peculate, purloin'. He notes the Septuagint uses it at Jos.7:1 for Hebrew לָקַח, take. The middle voice points to keeping it for himself, which the BSB spells out.

03.r: He took from the price, not the whole of it.

05.r: The money received for the property.
05.n: Abbott-Smith: 'a price paid or received', with a genitive of the thing, and he cites this verse and the next. The DRC adds 'of the land'.

06.r: His wife knew of the plan and shared in it.
06.n: A perfect participle from the verb Abbott-Smith lists under συνεῖδον, whose root picture is 'to see together'; in the perfect it means to know along with someone. The 'with' in it makes her a partner in the knowledge, as the Geneva's 'being of counsell' brings out.

08.r: The article, which here points to Ananias' own wife.
08.n: Our text has only the article, 'the wife'; English says 'his'. The 'his' of the older translations answers to the Textus Receptus's αὐτοῦ.

09.n: Abbott-Smith gives first 'a woman, married or unmarried'; here, with the article, his wife.

11.r: Joins what he kept to what he handed over.

12.r: He brought part of the money to the apostles.
12.n: An aorist participle: the bringing comes before the laying down. Abbott-Smith: 'to bear, carry'.

13.r: Only part of the sum, presented as if it were the whole.
13.n: Abbott-Smith: 'a part, share, portion', and 'a part as opposite to the whole'. That he presented it as the whole is a reading from the verses around this one, not stated in this verse.

14.r: Leaves the size of the part unstated.

15.r: Next to their feet, as others had done.
15.n: Abbott-Smith gives this preposition the root sense 'beside'. His entry for 'foot' records 'at the feet' with this preposition or with πρός.

17.r: Laying it at their feet hands it over to the apostles.

18.r: The article; 'of' comes from the genitive case of the noun that follows.

19.n: Abbott-Smith derives it from ἀποστέλλω, to send, and gives 'a messenger, one sent on a mission'.

20.r: He set the money down before the apostles.
20.n: Abbott-Smith: 'to place, lay, set'. The Greek holds the verb to the end, as the YLT keeps: 'at the feet of the apostles he laid it'.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus adds αὐτοῦ, 'of him', after 'the wife', which is the KJV's 'his wife'. Our text has only the article; English says 'his wife' either way.
